blocks.title: "Delivered" (it wasn't)
blocks.narration: It is Wednesday morning, and Leo has just forwarded you an angry email. Elena ordered a climbing rope for a climbing trip this weekend. Last night she asked Scout whether it had arrived, and Scout told her it had been delivered. It hadn't: the carrier shows it still in transit. And Scout's log shows no errors at all. So before anything is explained: why did Scout say delivered?
blocks.why: Scout has been answering tracking questions for a week. Last night it told a customer her parcel had arrived. It hadn't, and this morning she wants to know why Orbit lied to her.
blocks.stat: 1 parcel still in transit · 1 reply saying "delivered" · 0 errors in the log

blocks.prompt: Before anything is explained: why did Scout tell Elena her rope was delivered?

hunches.label: ParcelPath briefly sent Scout wrong data that said "delivered"
The tracking call failed, the error was hidden, and Scout filled the gap
Scout looked up the wrong order and read another customer's status

reveal.narration: Here is what really happened. Elena asked about her order, and Scout called get order, which worked and returned her tracking number. Then Scout called track parcel, but ParcelPath was slow, and the call timed out. The code caught the timeout and quietly returned an empty string, with no error flag and nothing in the log. To Scout, that looked like a tool that worked and had nothing new to say. Her rope had shipped six days earlier on three to five day shipping, so Scout filled the gap with the likeliest story: delivered.

frames.caption: Elena asks Scout whether her rope from order ORB-10560 has arrived.
Scout calls get_order. It works: shipped six days ago with ParcelPath, standard shipping, tracking PP-90417.
Scout calls track_parcel for the latest scan. ParcelPath is slow, and the call times out after 10 seconds.
The code catches the timeout and returns "": no is_error, nothing logged. The failure is now invisible to Scout.
To Scout, an empty result reads as "worked, nothing new". Six days in, on 3-to-5-day shipping, it guesses: delivered.
The reply goes out: "Good news, your rope has been delivered!" It is still in transit, out of the Denver hub.

The reply goes out: "Good news, your rope has been delivered!" It is still in transit, out of the Denver hub.

blocks.wrap_correct: Right. The tracking call failed, but the code turned the timeout into an empty string. Scout couldn't tell "the lookup failed" from "nothing to report", so it filled the gap with the likeliest story.
blocks.wrap_wrong: Not quite. ParcelPath's data was right, and get_order found the right order. The tracking call timed out, and the code returned an empty string instead of an error. Scout never knew the lookup had failed, so it guessed.
blocks.wrap_point: Tools give Scout real facts, but only if every failure is reported back to it as an error, never hidden.

blocks.title: Give your agent a calculator and a file reader
blocks.situation: Leo's team spends hours on two kinds of question: "how much will I get back?" and "what does the policy say?". Scout can talk about both, but it does sums in its head and has never read Orbit's policy file. Today you give it a calculator, a file reader, and the loop that lets it use them.
blocks.intro: By the end you'll have tools.py with two safe tools and agent.py running the tool loop, with errors reported back to Scout instead of hidden.

items: Your **scout** folder from Modules 1 and 2, with the virtual environment active (`.venv\Scripts\activate` on Windows, `source .venv/bin/activate` on macOS and Linux)
The **anthropic** package installed and **ANTHROPIC_API_KEY** set in this terminal

steps.title: Add Orbit's policy file
steps.body: Scout's file reader will only open files in one folder, docs. Start by putting Orbit's policy there.
actions: In your **scout** folder, create a folder for documents: run `mkdir docs`.
Inside **docs**, create a file called **policy.md**.
Paste the text below and save.

values.label: docs/policy.md
values.value:
# Orbit Outdoor policies
## Returns
You can return any unused item within 30 days of delivery for a full refund. Items must be unused and in their original packaging.
## Return shipping
Return shipping is free on orders over $75. Under $75, a $6.95 return label is taken off the refund.
## Refunds
Refunds go back to the original payment method within 5 business days of the return arriving. Refunds over $200 must be approved by a member of the support team.
## Exchanges
Exchanging for a different size is free if the new size is in stock.
## Shipping
Standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days. Express takes 1 to 2 business days.
## Damaged items
Send a photo within 7 days of delivery and we send a replacement or a full refund.

steps.check: From the **scout** folder, `python -c "print(open('docs/policy.md').read()[:24])"` prints `# Orbit Outdoor policies`.
steps.tip: On Windows, make sure the file is called policy.md and not policy.md.txt. Turn on **File name extensions** in File Explorer's **View** menu to check.

steps.title: Build a safe calculator
steps.body: Models are unreliable at exact arithmetic, so Scout will hand every sum to Python. This calculator parses the text with ast and allows only numbers and arithmetic. There is no eval, so no other code can ever run.
actions: Create **tools.py** in the **scout** folder.
Paste the code below and save.
Try a sum: `python -c "from tools import calculate; print(calculate('240 * 0.85'))"`.
Try something that isn't arithmetic: `python -c "from tools import calculate; calculate('open(1)')"`.

values.label: tools.py

steps.check: The first command prints `204.0`. The second ends with `ValueError: only numbers, + - * / ** and parentheses are allowed`: a function call was refused, not run.
steps.tip: `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tools'` means you're not in the scout folder. `cd` into it and run the command again.

steps.title: Add a file reader that stays inside docs
steps.body: read_file joins the name to the docs folder, resolves it to a full path, and refuses anything that ends up outside docs, such as ../tools.py.
actions: Open **tools.py** and paste the code below at the bottom, after a blank line.
Save, then read the policy: `python -c "from tools import read_file; print(read_file('policy.md')[:60])"`.
Now try to escape the folder: `python -c "from tools import read_file; read_file('../tools.py')"`.

values.label: tools.py (add at the bottom)

steps.check: The first command prints the start of the policy, beginning `# Orbit Outdoor policies`. The second ends with `ValueError: ../tools.py is outside the docs folder`.
steps.tip: `Path(__file__).parent` is the folder tools.py lives in, so read_file finds docs no matter which folder you start Python from.

steps.title: Describe the tools and add a dispatcher
steps.body: The model never sees your Python. It sees TOOLS: a name, a description and an input schema for each tool. run_tool maps each name to its function, so a tool request becomes a real call.
actions: Paste the code below at the bottom of **tools.py**, after a blank line, and save.
Run a tool the way the agent will: `python -c "from tools import run_tool; print(run_tool('calculate', {'expression': '240 * 15 / 100'}))"`.

values.label: tools.py (add at the bottom)

steps.check: It prints `36.0`. That is the exact path the agent will use: a tool name and an input dictionary in, text out.
steps.tip: The descriptions are prompts. If Scout later skips a tool or picks the wrong one, improve the description before you change any code.

steps.title: Write the tool loop
steps.body: agent.py sends the question with TOOLS, runs every tool Scout asks for, and sends all the results back in one message. Failures go back with is_error, and MAX_STEPS = 6 stops a runaway loop.
actions: Create **agent.py** in the **scout** folder.
Paste the code below and save.
Read the loop once. It is the loop from the lessons, plus two `print` lines so you can watch each tool call, and a polite fallback if the step limit runs out.
Check that it loads: `python -c "import agent"`.

values.label: agent.py
values.value:
import sys

import anthropic

from tools import TOOLS, run_tool

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"
MAX_STEPS = 6  # the most model calls one question may use

SYSTEM = """You are Scout, Orbit Outdoor's support assistant.
Use the calculate tool for every sum, discount or refund amount. Never do arithmetic in your head.
Use the read_file tool to check Orbit's policy in policy.md before answering any policy question.
Only state facts that come from a tool result or from the customer.
If a tool returns an error, do not guess. Say plainly what you could not check, and offer to pass the question to a person on the team.
Keep replies short, friendly and plain."""


def ask(question):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for step in range(MAX_STEPS):                       # always a step limit
        response = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=16000,
                                          system=SYSTEM, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            break
        results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type == "tool_use":
                print(f"  [tool] {block.name}({block.input})")
                try:
                    output = run_tool(block.name, block.input)
                    results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": output})
                except Exception as err:
                    print(f"  [error] {err}")
                    results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                                    "content": f"Error: {err}", "is_error": True})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})   # all results in one message
    if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":              # still asking for tools: the step limit ran out
        return "Sorry, I couldn't finish that one. I'll pass your question to a person on the team."
    return next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    question = " ".join(sys.argv[1:]) or input("Ask Scout: ")
    print(ask(question))

steps.check: The import prints nothing and shows no error. Your **scout** folder now holds **docs/policy.md**, **tools.py** and **agent.py**.
steps.tip: An IndentationError usually means the `try` and `except` lines aren't inside the `for block in response.content:` loop. Compare your indentation with the code above, line by line.

steps.title: Ask Scout to do a sum
steps.body: Now watch the loop work. Scout should hand the arithmetic to calculate instead of doing it in its head.
actions: Run `python agent.py "What is 15 percent off a 240 dollar tent?"`.
Watch for the `[tool]` lines that appear before the answer.
steps.check: You see at least one line like `[tool] calculate({'expression': '240 * 0.85'})`, then an answer of 204 dollars. Scout may work out the 36 dollar discount first, so two calculate calls are fine too.
steps.tip: No `[tool]` line means Scout did the sum in its head. Check that `tools=TOOLS` is in the create call and that SYSTEM tells Scout to use calculate for every sum.

steps.title: Ask about the policy
steps.body: This time the answer lives in a file Scout has never seen, so it should reach for read_file.
actions: Run `python agent.py "What does our policy say about returns?"`.
steps.check: You see `[tool] read_file({'name': 'policy.md'})`, then an answer that mentions 30 days from delivery, unused items in their original packaging, and free return shipping on orders over 75 dollars.
steps.tip: `[error] no file called policy.md in docs` means the file is in the wrong place or has a hidden .txt ending. It must be **scout/docs/policy.md**.

steps.title: Break it on purpose
steps.body: Tools fail. Ask about a file that doesn't exist and watch the error travel back to Scout with is_error, instead of being hidden the way Elena's tracking error was.
actions: Run `python agent.py "What does warranty.md in our docs say about tents?"`.
Read the `[error]` line, then Scout's answer.
steps.check: You see `[tool] read_file({'name': 'warranty.md'})` and `[error] no file called warranty.md in docs`. Scout says it couldn't find a warranty file and doesn't invent warranty terms. It may also open policy.md to look, which is fine: there is no warranty section there either.
steps.tip: If Scout describes a warranty anyway, check that your except block sets `"is_error": True` and that SYSTEM tells Scout not to guess when a tool fails.

finish.title: Scout can calculate, read, and admit what it doesn't know
finish.body: You built two safe tools, described them for the model, and ran the full tool loop with a step limit. When a tool failed, the error reached Scout with is_error, and it answered honestly instead of guessing. In Module 4 you'll give Scout memory and a search_policy tool that finds the right part of the policy.
checklist: **tools.py** has calculate (ast, no eval) and read_file (docs only)
TOOLS describes both tools, and run_tool maps each name to its function
**agent.py** runs the tool loop with MAX_STEPS = 6
Tool failures go back as a tool_result with is_error true
Scout answered a sum, a policy question and a missing file correctly

blocks.title: Which tool, and what if it fails?
blocks.intro: Three situations from Scout's first week with tools. In each one, decide what should change, or what Scout should do.

scenarios.title: Scout searches instead of looking up
scenarios.situation: Priya added a search_help tool that searches Orbit's help pages. Since then, when customers give an order number, Scout often searches the help pages instead of calling get_order, and replies with general shipping advice. Ravi, whose order is still processing, was told it should arrive in 3 to 5 days. Leo pasted the two tool descriptions and a trace.

context.label: Tool descriptions and Scout's trace
lines: search_help: "Search Orbit's help pages for answers to
user> Where's my order ORB-10533? It's been 4 days.
< Standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days...
scout> Orders usually arrive in 3 to 5 business days.

options.text: Rewrite get_order's description: look up one Orbit order by its ID, like ORB-10482, and use it whenever a customer gives an order number
options.rationale: The model chooses tools by their descriptions. "Gets data" says nothing, while search_help sounds like it covers orders. A clear what-and-when description makes get_order the obvious choice.

options.text: Delete search_help, so get_order is the only tool left
options.rationale: That stops this mistake but throws away a useful tool. The real problem is that get_order's description gives the model no reason to pick it.

options.text: Add a system prompt rule: call get_order first for every message, no matter what
options.rationale: Calling get_order on every message wastes calls and fails when there's no order number. Fix the description so the model knows when get_order fits.

hints: Read the two descriptions as if you were the model. Which one sounds like it handles order questions?
The model never sees your Python, only the descriptions.

scenarios.debrief: When an agent picks the wrong tool, read the tool descriptions first: they are prompts. Say what each tool does, when to use it and what the input looks like, and make overlapping tools clearly different. Then rerun the same question to confirm the fix.

scenarios.title: The tracking API is down for 20 minutes
scenarios.situation: At 2:00 PM on Tuesday, ParcelPath's API starts timing out on every call. It comes back at 2:20, but for twenty minutes every tracking question hits the outage. track_parcel already retries twice with backoff, then raises an error that the loop returns with is_error. At 2:07, Ana asks where her tent is.

context.label: Scout's trace, 2:07 PM
lines: user> Where's my tent? Order ORB-10482
< is_error: ParcelPath timed out 3 times. Status unknown.

options.text: Nothing yet: keep retrying track_parcel until ParcelPath comes back
options.rationale: Ana would wait up to twenty minutes while the loop burns through its step limit and your money. Retries are for brief blips, not outages.

options.text: Her tent is in transit and should arrive within 3 to 5 business days
options.rationale: It sounds helpful, but the live status is unknown. This is Elena's mistake again: a guess presented as a fact.

options.text: It shipped with ParcelPath (tracking PP-88213), but live tracking is down right now; she can check later, or Scout can pass her question to the team
options.rationale: It shares what Scout does know from get_order, is honest about what it doesn't, and gives Ana a way forward. Nothing is guessed.

hints: Separate what Scout knows from get_order from what it doesn't know.
Retries help with a blip of a few seconds. Is a twenty-minute outage a blip?

scenarios.debrief: Retry briefly inside the tool, then report the error with is_error and let the model handle it honestly. Scout should share the facts it has, say plainly what it couldn't check, and offer a next step. In production, also alert the team when the same tool fails many times in a row.

scenarios.title: 4,000 lines for one parcel
scenarios.situation: Priya's first version of track_parcel returns ParcelPath's whole response as text. For most parcels that's about 4,000 lines of JSON: every scan event, depot codes, route IDs and driver notes. Scout's replies have become slow and expensive, and yesterday one reply quoted a driver's note about a customer's gate code.

context.label: track_parcel result (first lines of 4,012)
lines: "driver_notes": "gate code 4471, dog in yard, leave at side door",

question.stem: What should track_parcel return to Scout?

options.text: The full response, plus a system prompt rule telling Scout never to mention driver notes
options.rationale: The rule may work most of the time, but you still pay for 4,000 lines on every call, and the private data still sits in the model's context. Remove it in code instead.

options.text: Only the status, the estimated delivery and the last scan, as a short JSON string
options.rationale: Those fields answer the tracking questions customers actually ask. Fewer tokens means faster, cheaper replies, and private fields like driver notes never reach the model or the customer.

options.text: The full response, so Scout always has every detail it might need
options.rationale: That's what is happening now: slow, costly replies and private notes leaking into answers. More context isn't better when most of it is noise.

hints: List the questions customers actually ask about tracking. Which fields answer them?
Which is safer: asking the model not to repeat something, or never giving it to the model at all?

scenarios.debrief: Treat a tool's output like a prompt you are writing: include what the model needs and nothing else. Trimming in code is cheaper and safer than asking the model to ignore things, and it keeps private fields away from customers. If Scout later needs one more field, add that one field.

items.stem: A customer returns a $58 order. Policy takes the $6.95 return label off orders under $75, and Scout replies, "You'll get $51.15 back." The right figure is $51.05. What is the best fix?

items.stem: Priya is connecting ParcelPath's tracking API so Scout can answer "where is my parcel?" questions. Which way of giving Scout access is the safest, and the easiest for the model to use well?

options.text: A track_parcel tool that takes a tracking number; your code adds the key and a timeout

variants.stem: At 8 PM on Black Friday, track_parcel starts getting 429 responses with Retry-After: 3. Customers are waiting in the chat. What should your code do?

options.text: Wait the 3 seconds and retry a couple of times, cache recent lookups, and if it still fails, return is_error so Scout can explain
